entry.title: Logic Bug in XNU Kernel Affects UNIX Domain Socket Inodes
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | yuvalino.com | discussion | hacker news

A technical demo crash on an iOS device revealed a decades-old logic bug in how the XNU kernel assigns inodes to UNIX domain sockets. The issue resides in the `uipc_sense()` function, where a post-increment error causes the first socket created after a system boot to be assigned an inode of 0. This inconsistency causes subsequent `fstat()` calls to return different inode numbers, leading to failures in software that requires stable inode identification.

The bug's origins trace back to 1985 in the 4.3BSD source code, having survived through the NeXTSTEP era and into modern macOS and iOS versions. While not a security vulnerability, the flaw demonstrates how legacy code from the early Unix era has persisted through decades of operating system evolution.

entry.title: The Origin of the x86 ud2 Instruction Name
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | devblogs.microsoft.com | hacker news

The ud2 instruction is an architecturally undefined x86 instruction designed to trigger an "invalid opcode" exception. Compilers use it to mark unreachable code, ensuring that if execution flow erroneously reaches such a point, the program crashes immediately rather than executing unintended instructions.

The instruction's name is a result of the retroactive naming of previous, unofficial methods used to trigger the exception. Developers previously relied on the 0F FF and 0F B9 byte sequences to force invalid opcodes; as Intel formalized these behaviors, the 0F FF and 0F B9 sequences were designated ud0 and ud1, respectively, leaving ud2 as the standard, parameter-free instruction.

entry.title: Rust Stabilizes Never Type
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | lwn.net | discussion | hacker news

Rust is stabilizing its "never" type (`!`), which represents values that can never occur or functions that never return. The feature enables more efficient generic code by allowing the compiler to optimize away unreachable error branches in infallible conversions and simplifies type inference for expressions like infinite loops. As part of this update, the standard library's `Infallible` type will become a type alias for the never type.

The change introduces a breaking change in how the compiler handles type inference fallback, shifting the default from the unit type `()` to `!`. While this could impact several thousand crates, many have already been addressed through community patches or backports discovered using the `crater` tool. Developers can resolve potential compilation errors by explicitly specifying return types or updating to supported dependency versions.

This discrepancy poses a risk for long-term, iterative development, as poor coding decisions accumulate when using automated agents.

Quantitative metrics such as verbosity and erosion demonstrate that AI-generated code is significantly more verbose and complex than human-authored repositories. Benchmarks like SlopCodeBench, which simulate real-world iterative development by resetting model context between instruction rounds, show that even state-of-the-art models struggle to maintain quality over long-horizon tasks, often failing to pass cumulative tests as complexity increases.

Analysis of the YAML 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2 specifications and historical mailing list archives indicates that these errors stem from a reliance on unsafe deserialization defaults. entry.title: ACPI SystemIO Conflicts Are Not Always Firmware Bugs
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | codon.org.uk | discussion

ACPI SystemIO range conflict warnings do not necessarily indicate a firmware bug. These errors occur when the kernel detects an overlap between a hardware driver attempting to access an I/O port and an ACPI OpRegion claiming those same addresses. This detection serves as a safety mechanism to prevent race conditions that occur when the firmware and the operating system attempt to manipulate the same hardware registers simultaneously.

Such conflicts can lead to hardware errors, such as reading incorrect status flags or triggering unintended thermal shutdowns. While the kernel may block conflicting drivers to mitigate these risks, the most reliable way to interact with the hardware is through the ACPI-provided methods and drivers provided by the firmware.
